background.definition: Testicular cancer is the most common solid malignant tumor in young men; 95% are germ cell tumors (GCTs).

list.listitem: The incidence of testicular cancer has risen steadily over the past 50 years.
Approximately 8250 new cases each year in United States with 370 deaths.
The incidence of GCT increases after puberty and peaks in the fourth decade of life, with a median age at diagnosis of 34 years.
4 to 10 per 100,000 in men of Northern European descent.
0.2 to 1 per 100,000 Asian, African, and African-American men.
Testicular cancer is the most common solid malignant tumor in young men.
Testicular cancer represents 1% of all male cancers and 0.1% of cancer deaths.
The etiology of testicular cancer is poorly understood.
Environmental factors, in utero estrogen concentrations, familial predisposition, and duplication of the short arm of chromosome 12 have all been implicated in the etiology of testicular cancer.
A systematic review of observational studies found that boys with isolated cryptorchidism are at increased risk for testicular cancer (RR 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8).
95% of all testicular cancers are germ cell tumors (GCTs), which are comprised of seminomatous (immature germ cells) and nonseminomatous (mature germ cell) cancers.

Nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCTs) generally contain two or more cell types (of which one might be seminoma). Other cell types include embryonal carcinoma, teratoma, yolk-sac tumor, and choriocarcinoma.
50% of testicular GCTs are pure seminomas.
The remaining 5% of testicular cancers are non-germ cell tumors and consist of sex-cord stromal, mixed, adnexal, and paratesticular tumors.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Prior history of testicular cancer or extragonadal germ cell tumor

list.listitem: The USPSTF recommends against routine screening for testicular cancer in asymptomatic adolescent and adult males, including self-examination (D recommendation). B

A Cochrane review found no RCTs of screening, but recommends informing patients at increased risk due to family history, cryptorchidism, or testicular atrophy of their risk and options for surveillance. C
The Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine does recommend a male genital examiantion as part of a routine physical, based on expert opinion. C
The European Association of Urology recommends that young men be informed about the importance of physical self-examination, especially in those with a family history of testicular cancer. C
Men presenting with a solid, firm testicular mass are presumed to have testicular cancer until proven otherwise. C
Scrotal ultrasound is the recommended intial diagnostic test in men with suspected testicular cancer to distinguish between lesions that are intrinsic or extrinsic to the testicle. C
Radical inguinal orchiectomy is recommended for men with testicular mass for histologic evaluation. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Sudden onset of pain and swelling; ipsilateral testical often elevated
Subacute onset of pain and swelling; urethral discharge and irritative voiding symptoms common; inflammatory cells on urinalysis
Painless swelling in scrotum; transillumination can be helpful
Painless swelling in scrotum; palpable "bag of worms" along spermatic cord
Scrotal mass that can vary in size due to presence of abdominal contents; defect in inguinal ring seen on physical examination
Pain and swelling in scrotum; history of antecedent trauma (or scrotal surgery) common
Painless mass superior and anterior to testes

list.listitem: The most common presentation of testicular cancer is an incidentally noted painless testicular mass or swelling. Men presenting with a solid, firm testicular mass are presumed to have testicular cancer until proven otherwise.
One in three patients will present with a dull ache in the ipsilateral testicle.
Ask patient for history of undescended testicle, trauma, prior scrotal infections, prior scrotal surgeries, pain, weight loss, fever, or chills.

Physical examination includes bilateral scrotal examination along with examination of the chest, abdomen, and lymphatic system to look for gynecomastia, abnormal breath sounds, abdominal masses, or lymphadenopathy.

A case control study with 1398 men with testicular cancer and 4956 matched controls found that testicular swelling (OR 280), testicular lump (OR 270), and scrotal swelling (OR 170) were the strongest predictors of cancer. The positive predictive value of a testicular lump was 2.5% for cancer. The combination of a testicular lump plus swelling or pain had positive predictive values of 17% and 10% respectively.

Scrotal ultrasound (USN) is useful as an intial diagnostic test in men with suspected testicular cancer to disinguish between lesions that are intrinsic or extrinsic to the testicle. It is useful to confirm the presence of an intratesticular mass and to examine the contralateral testis.

Ultrasound is nearly 100% sensitive for detecting tumors of the testis as small as 1 to 2 mm. All patients with intrinsic testicular mass should have inguinal exploration with exteriorization of the testis and frozen sections for histology if the diagnosis is in question or immediate orchiectomy if it is not.

A study of multiparametric USN (which combines gray-scale USN, color Doppler USN, strain elastrography, and contrast enhanced USN) was 100% sensitive and 93% specific for differentiating malignant from benign lesions.
When ultrasound is inconclusive, consider MRI of the testes.
CBC, urinalysis, and basic serum chemistries and urethral cultures provide baseline renal function data and ensure there is no concurrent infection.
Perform CXR before treatment of men with suspected germ cell tumors (GCTs) to look for metastatic disease.

Obtain three serum tumor markers in men with suspected testicular cancer: beta human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG), alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Patients with NSGCTs will have elevation of beta-HCG and AFP in most cases. Patients with pure seminomatous GCTs rarely have AFP elevation. While serum tumor markers are not diagnostic of testicular cancer, men rarely have significant elevations in clinical settings other than testicular cancer.
Histology from surgical specimens will differentiate between seminoma and nonseminomatous testicular tumors.

Perform high-resolution CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis at baseline before treatment of confirmed testicular cancer for staging. Use MRI if patients cannot tolerate IV contrast., although AUA guidelines recommend against use of MRI for initial evaluation and diagnosis of lesions suspicious for cancer.
Consider cerebral or spinal imaging in patients with multiple lung metastases or suggestive clinical symptoms.
Consider biopsy of the contralateral testis particularly in patients with higher risk (small testicular volume, <12 mL; history of cryptorchidism; or age less than 30).
Patients typically present with a painless testicular mass.

Ultrasound is a good initial diagnostic test to confirm that a mass is intrinsic to the testicle, but it is not reliable for distinguishing benign from malignant lesions. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is necessary for histologic evaluation.
Patients with normal HCG and AFP and indeterminate ultrasound should undergo repeat ultrasound in 2 months.
Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) is the standard in the United States to provide disease staging (see ).
Radical inguinal orchiectomy is recommended for men with suspected testicular cancer for histologic evaluation. B
Post orchidectomy options for men with stage 1 seminoma include surveillance, radiotherapy, or single-agent chemotherapy.
Patients with stage 2 seminoma are preferentially treated with radiation therapy.

Factors including histopathology, serum biomarkers, clinical stage of disease, and patient/physician preference determine how individual patients will be treated. Treatment options for testicular cancer include surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and surveillance. Once the diagnosis of testicular cancer is made, treatment depends on the stage of disease ().

Radical inguinal orchiectomy is recommended for men with suspected testicular cancer for histologic evaluation. Transscrotal orchiectomy is not recommended. Patients should discuss testicular prosthesis prior to surgery with their surgeon.
Testis sparing surgery is an option only for carefully selected patients with <2 cm mass, equivocal ultrasound findings, and negative tumor markers.
Semen cryopreservation should be offered to men desiring to preserve options for fertility.
Men should be offered a testicular prosthesis pre-operatively.
5% of patients will have intratubular germ cell neoplasia (ITGCN), unclassified (the precursor to invasive GCTs) in the contralateral testicle.

Post orchidectomy options for men with stage 1 seminoma include surveillance, radiotherapy, and single-agent chemotherapy. For patients choosing surveillance, 15% to 20% of stage 1 seminomas will recur after orchidectomy. Recurrence for patients treated with adjuvant irradiation or adjuvant chemotherapy is 3% to 4%. Treatment with radiation or chemotherapy following relapse of clinical stage 1 seminoma results in cure rates of over 99%.
Treat patients who have stage 2 seminoma preferentially with radiation therapy. Seminomas are very radiosensitive. Para-aortic field radiation is the current treatment of choice.

For non-seminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT), in the United States most patients undergo retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. In Europe, patients with NSGCT are also offered surveillance and chemotherapy. Clinical outcomes of all three approaches are similar.

AUA 2019 guidelines for treatment of early stage testicular cancer recommend the following treatments by stage:
Stage IA: Preferred option is surveillance, with retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) or 1 round of bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin (BEP) chemotherapy. Stage IB: Options include surveillance, RPLND, or 1 round of BEP chemotherapy. Stage IIA: Options include RPLND or risk-appropriate multi-agent cisplatin-based chemotherapy. Stage IIB: Preferred option is risk-appropriate, multi-agent cisplatin-based chemotherapy, with RPLND as an alternative.
AUA 2019 guidelines recommend multi-agent cisplatin-based chemotherapy for patients with Stage 1, IIA or IIB disease and rising AFP or HCG levels post-orchiectomy.
Treatment of advanced metastatic seminoma and NSGCT is chemotherapy based. Platinum based chemotherapy has a high response rate.
In the setting of relapsed disease refractory to standard chemotherapy there are indications that immunotherapy may be effective.

Non-seminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT): follow up with clinic visits, CXR, and tumor markers. Perform CT of the chest and abdomen quarterly for 1 year after diagnosis and once again at 24 months after diagnosis. 30% of stage 1 NSGCTs will recur; 99% of these are cured by chemotherapy. B

Seminoma: 80% of patients with seminoma are cured by orchidectomy alone. Follow up serially with CXR and tumor markers (looking for mixed tumors, as tumor markers are less informative in patients with seminoma). Patients who have a normal CT after receiving adjuvant treatment with chemotherapy or radiation therapy do not require further CT follow-up. 85% have stage 1 disease, and 15% will relapse within 4 years without adjuvant therapy. B
The overall prognosis for seminoma and NSGCT is good. B

A retrospective cohort review of 1754 cancer survivors with 7117 controls demonstrated increased risk of both erectile dysfunction and testosterone deficiency in the testis cancer patients. While stratification by receipt of chemotherapy showed no difference, it is clear that for those receiving chemotherapy survivorship requires support with regard to sexual function.
Elevated c-reactive protein is a predictor of relapse or complications.

A series of 1447 patients with Stage 1 germ cell cancer found 159 relapses, none of which were identified on CXR; therefore, the authors only recommend tumor markers and CT are recommended for follow-up.

feature.caption: Staging of Testicular Cancer.
feature.feature_body:
Stage Description
Primary Tumor (P)
pTx Primary tumor cannot be assessed
pT0 No evidence of tumor
pTis Intratubular tumor (carcinoma in situ)
pT1 Tumor limited to testis
pT2 Tumor extends outside the tunica albuginea or vascular/lymphatic invasion
pT3 Tumor invades spermatic cord
pT4 Tumor invades scrotum
Regional Lymph Nodes (pN)
pNx Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed
pN0 No lymph node metastasis
pN1 Metastasis to fewer than 5 nodes, none >2 cm OR lymph node mass <2 cm
pN2 Metastasis to more than 5 nodes, none >5 cm OR lymph node mass >2 cm but less than 5 cm; OR extranodal extension
pN3 Lymph node mass >5 cm
Distant Metastasis (M)
Mx Distant metastasis cannot be assessed
M0 No distant metastasis
M1 Distant metastases present
M1a Nonregional lymph node or pulmonary metastases
M1b Other distant metastases
Serum Tumor Markers (S)
Sx Marker studies unavailable or not performed
S0 Serum tumor markers within normal limits
S1 LDH <1.5 ULN AND beta-hCG <5,000 mIU/mL AND AFP <1,000 ng/mL
S2 LDH 1.5-10 ULN OR 5,000 mIU/mL < beta-hCG < 50,000 mIU/mL OR 1,000 ng/mL < AFP < 10,000 ng/mL
S3 LDH >10x ULN OR beta-hCG >50,000 OR AFP >10,000 ng/mL
Clinical Stage Primary Tumor Regional Nodes Distant Metastases Serum Markers
0 pTis N0 M0 S0
I pT1-4 N0 M0 Sx
IA pT1 N0 M0 S0
IB pT2-4 N0 M0 S0
IS Any pT or Tx N0 M0 S1-3
II Any pT or Tx N1-3 M0 Sx
IIA Any pT or Tx N1 M0 S0-1
IIB Any pT or Tx N2 M0 S0-1
IIC Any pT or Tx N3 M0 S0-1
III Any pT or Tx Any N M1a Sx
IIIA Any pT or Tx Any N M1a S0-1
IIIB Any pT or Tx Any N M1a S2
IIIC Any pT or Tx Any N M1b S3
